question_interpretation: Asks (1) who is subject to 21 CFR Part 117 and (2) what the principal exemptions are.

issues.detail: J answers only the exemptions half. The 'who is subject' half is not addressed: Subpart B CGMP applies to establishments that manufacture, process, pack or hold food (117.1, 117.4(a)(1), 117.10 'management of the establishment'), while Subparts C, D, E, F and G apply to the owner/operator/agent in charge of a 'facility', i.e. a domestic or foreign facility required to register under FD&C Act section 415 / 21 CFR part 1 subpart H (117.3 'Facility'; 117.1(b); 117.4(a)(2)).

J does not say that almost all 117.5 exemptions are exemptions from Subparts C and G only (the facility still must meet Subpart B CGMP), and that the qualified-facility 'exemption' is not a full exemption: qualified facilities are subject to the modified requirements in 117.201 (117.5(a)) and the exemption can be withdrawn under Subpart E. Subpart B itself does not apply to farms, certain fishing vessels, RAC-only holders/transporters, and nut hullers/shellers (117.5(k)).

Other principal exemptions omitted: LACF microbiological hazards under part 113 (117.5(d)), dietary supplements in compliance with part 111 (117.5(e)), produce-safety activities under section 419 (117.5(f)), alcoholic beverages (117.5(i)), storage-only of non-produce RACs (117.5(j)), and storage of unexposed packaged food (117.7, which routes TCS food to 117.206).

explanation: The listed exemptions (qualified facilities, juice HACCP part 120, seafood HACCP part 123, low-risk on-farm activity/food combinations) all exist in 117.5. But the question has two parts and J omits who is subject to Part 117 (117.1/117.3 'facility' registration trigger vs. Subpart B establishment-wide CGMP) and does not convey that the 117.5 exemptions are from Subparts C and G only, with qualified facilities still subject to 117.201. The citation omits 117.1, 117.3 and 117.7.
proposed_corrected_answer: Who is subject: Part 117 Subpart B CGMP applies to establishments that manufacture, process, pack, or hold human food (management of the establishment), subject to the 117.5(k) exclusions (farms, certain fishing vessels, establishments solely holding/transporting RACs, nut hulling/shelling/drying). Subparts C-G (hazard analysis and risk-based preventive controls, modified requirements, withdrawal, records, supply-chain) apply to the owner, operator, or agent in charge of a 'facility' — a domestic or foreign facility required to register under FD&C Act section 415 (part 1, subpart H). Principal exemptions from Subparts C and G (117.5): qualified facilities (instead subject to modified requirements in 117.201, exemption withdrawable under Subpart E); activities in compliance with seafood HACCP (part 123) or juice HACCP (part 120); microbiological hazards controlled under the LACF regulation (part 113); dietary supplements in compliance with part 111 and FD&C Act 761; activities subject to the produce safety standards (section 419); low-risk on-farm packing/holding and manufacturing/processing activity/food combinations by small or very small businesses on farm mixed-type facilities; certain alcoholic beverage facilities; facilities solely storing non-produce RACs; and (117.7) facilities solely storing unexposed packaged food (subject only to 117.206 for TCS food).

question_interpretation: Asks for the definition of 'qualified facility' and the modified requirements that apply to such a facility.

issues.detail: J says only 'modified requirements in lieu of a full food safety plan' and does not state what they are: attestation that it is a qualified facility plus either a hazard-control attestation or a non-Federal food safety law compliance attestation (117.201(a)), submission every 2 years (Oct 1-Dec 31, beginning 2020), annual status determination by July 1, consumer notification of the facility name/address if no hazard-control attestation (117.201(e)), and supporting records (117.201(f)).

The definition has two alternative prongs: (i) a very small business (<$1,000,000 average annual human-food sales plus market value of food held without sale, 3-year average, inflation-adjusted), or (ii) a facility whose direct sales to qualified end-users exceed sales to all others AND whose average annual food sales are < $500,000 (inflation-adjusted). 'Tied to average annual sales thresholds' omits the qualified end-user prong and the dollar figures.

'Subpart D' also contains 117.206 (storage of unexposed packaged food), which is not relevant; the governing modified-requirements section is 117.201. 117.3 'very small business' and 'qualified end-user' definitions are needed for the definition.

explanation: The definition and the existence of modified requirements are correctly located (117.3, 117.5(a), 117.201). But J does not identify the actual modified requirements (attestations, timing, consumer notification, records) and gives no thresholds, so an answer that never names the attestations would satisfy J. The definition's two prongs and dollar thresholds should be stated.
proposed_corrected_answer: Qualified facility (117.3): a facility (counting sales of subsidiaries/affiliates) that is either (a) a very small business — averaging < $1,000,000/yr (inflation-adjusted, 3-year average) in human food sales plus market value of food held without sale — or (b) a facility whose average annual value of food sold directly to qualified end-users exceeded that sold to all other purchasers over the preceding 3 years and whose average annual food sales were < $500,000 (inflation-adjusted). Under 117.5(a) Subparts C and G do not apply (except as provided by Subpart E); instead 117.201 requires: an attestation that it is a qualified facility, plus either (i) an attestation that it has identified potential hazards, is implementing preventive controls and monitoring them, or (ii) an attestation of compliance with State/local/tribal/other non-Federal (including foreign) food safety law; status determined annually by July 1; attestations submitted initially and then every 2 years (Oct 1-Dec 31, beginning 2020) electronically or on Form FDA 3942a; if no hazard-control attestation, consumer notification of the facility name and complete business address on the label or at point of purchase; records supporting the attestations (subject to Subpart F with exceptions in 117.301(c)). The exemption can be withdrawn under Subpart E.

question_interpretation: Asks how process controls, sanitation controls and food allergen controls differ under Part 117.

issues.detail: J lists generic features ('categories of preventive controls, written procedures, parameters and values, application to identified hazards') and does not state the distinction asked for. Process controls cover parameters during operations such as heat processing, acidifying, irradiating and refrigerating, with parameters and max/min values (117.135(c)(1)). Food allergen controls cover protection from allergen cross-contact and labeling so the food is not misbranded under 403(w) (117.135(c)(2)). Sanitation controls keep the facility sanitary against environmental pathogens, biological hazards from employee handling and allergen hazards: cleanliness of food-contact surfaces and prevention of cross-contact/cross-contamination (117.135(c)(3)).

The regulatory consequences of the categories also differ and are omitted. Allergen and sanitation controls need no validation (117.160(c)(1)-(2)). Non-conformance with allergen controls under 117.135(c)(2)(i) or sanitation controls under 117.135(c)(3)(i)-(ii) may be handled by timely corrections instead of corrective-action procedures (117.150(c)(1)). G cites only 117.135.
'Parameters and values' applies only to process controls; listed without attribution it can blur the distinction.

explanation: 117.135(c)(1)-(3) is the right core citation and nothing in J is false. But J does not state what distinguishes the three categories, which is the question, and omits the management-component differences in 117.160(c) and 117.150(c). An answer that merely lists preventive-control features would satisfy J.
proposed_corrected_answer: Process controls (117.135(c)(1)): procedures/practices/processes controlling parameters during operations such as heat processing, acidifying, irradiating, refrigerating; must include the parameters and the maximum/minimum values to which they are controlled; generally require validation (117.160). Food allergen controls (117.135(c)(2)): procedures to protect food from allergen cross-contact (storage, handling, use) and to ensure correct labeling so food is not misbranded under 403(w); no validation required (117.160(c)(1)). Sanitation controls (117.135(c)(3)): procedures to keep the facility sanitary to minimize/prevent environmental pathogens, biological hazards from employee handling and allergen hazards — cleanliness of food-contact surfaces and prevention of allergen cross-contact and cross-contamination from insanitary objects, personnel and raw product; no validation required (117.160(c)(2)). For allergen (c)(2)(i) and sanitation (c)(3)(i)-(ii) controls, timely corrections may substitute for corrective-action procedures (117.150(c)(1)). All must be written (117.135(b)) and are subject to monitoring/corrective action/verification as appropriate (117.140).

question_interpretation: Scenario: a metal detector (a preventive control for a physical hazard) fails mid-shift. Asks what Part 117 requires for corrective actions and corrections.

issues.detail: J omits the requirement that matters most in this scenario: all affected food must be prevented from entering commerce if the facility cannot ensure it is not adulterated under 402 or misbranded under 403(w) (117.150(a)(2)(iv); for unanticipated problems 117.150(b)(2)(i)). Food that ran past a failed metal detector may contain metal.

J says 'distinguish corrections from corrective actions' but not the rule. Corrections in lieu of corrective action are allowed only for allergen/sanitation control conditions (117.150(c)(1)) or a minor and isolated problem that does not directly impact product safety (117.150(c)(2)). A metal-detector failure on a physical-hazard control directly affects product safety, so the corrections exception generally will not apply.

Omitted: if no corrective action procedure was established for this failure, or the control proves ineffective, 117.150(b) applies (unanticipated food safety problem), including reanalysis of the food safety plan when appropriate (117.150(b)(2)(ii), 117.170(b)(3)). Records must be verified (117.155(a)(3)) and reviewed by a PCQI within 7 working days (117.165(a)(4)(i)).

explanation: 117.150 is the correct governing section and J's elements are supported. But J leaves out preventing affected product from entering commerce (117.150(a)(2)(iv)), the central obligation after a metal-detector failure, and does not state when corrections can replace corrective actions or the unanticipated-problem/reanalysis path.
proposed_corrected_answer: Under written corrective action procedures (117.150(a)), the facility must: identify and correct the problem (repair/replace the detector; re-establish control); reduce the likelihood of recurrence when necessary; evaluate all affected food (product run since the last successful check) for safety, e.g., re-screening; and prevent all affected food from entering commerce if it cannot ensure the food is not adulterated (402) or misbranded (403(w)). If no procedure covered this failure, or the control is found ineffective, the same actions are required as an unanticipated food safety problem and, when appropriate, the food safety plan must be reanalyzed (117.150(b); 117.170). 'Corrections' (117.3) — identifying and correcting without the other corrective-action steps — are permitted only for allergen/sanitation control nonconformances or a minor, isolated problem that does not directly impact product safety (117.150(c)); a metal-detector failure ordinarily does not qualify. All corrective actions (and corrections when appropriate) must be documented, verified (117.155(a)(3)) and reviewed within 7 working days (117.165(a)(4)(i)).

They are: the hazard analysis, including the nature of the hazard controlled before receipt; the entity applying the controls; supplier performance (procedures, FDA compliance history such as warning letters and import alerts, food safety history); and other factors such as storage and transport. For qualified facilities, non-covered produce farms and small shell-egg producers, supplier performance may be limited to compliance history (117.410(d)(2)) and alternative written-assurance verification applies (117.430(c)-(e)).

G cites 117.420 (approved suppliers), which is peripheral, and omits 117.425 (determining activities), 117.435 (onsite audit by a qualified auditor; FDA/State inspection within 1 year may substitute) and 117.415(b) (the receiving facility may not accept the supplier's own audit or self-determination).

question_interpretation: Asks how the Part 117 Subpart G supply-chain program differs from the FSVP requirements for importers in 21 CFR part 1 subpart L.

issues.detail: 'Domestic receiving facility' is imprecise. A receiving facility is any facility subject to Subparts C and G that manufactures/processes a raw material received from a supplier (117.3), and 'facility' includes foreign facilities required to register (117.3). The real difference is the obligated party and trigger: a manufacturing/processing receiving facility (domestic or foreign) controlling supplier-applied hazards in its ingredients, versus the importer (U.S. owner or consignee at entry, or designated U.S. agent; 1.500) for each food imported.

J does not name the two non-duplication provisions. (1) 117.405(a)(2): a receiving facility that is an importer, complies with FSVP and has documentation of verification under 1.506(e) need not conduct supplier verification for that raw material. (2) 1.502(c): an importer that is a receiving facility complying with 117.135 preventive controls, 117.136, or a Subpart G supply-chain program for the food is deemed compliant with FSVP, except for the importer-identification-at-entry requirement in 1.509.

Substantive differences are omitted. FSVP covers each imported food and requires a hazard analysis (1.504), evaluation and approval of foreign suppliers with reevaluation at least every 3 years (1.505), and importer identification at entry (1.509). The supply-chain program applies only to raw materials with a hazard requiring a supply-chain-applied control. Both require an annual onsite audit for SAHCODHA hazards unless a written determination supports alternatives (1.506(d)(2); 117.430(b)).

explanation: G correctly points to Part 117 Subpart G and Part 1 Subpart L. J's 'domestic receiving facility vs importer' framing is imprecise, because Part 117 receiving facilities may be foreign, and J does not identify the specific non-duplication provisions (117.405(a)(2); 1.502(c), with the 1.509 carve-out) or any substantive difference.
proposed_corrected_answer: Part 117 Subpart G binds a receiving facility (a registered facility, domestic or foreign, subject to Subparts C and G that manufactures/processes a received raw material) to have a written, risk-based supply-chain program only for raw materials/ingredients with a hazard requiring a supply-chain-applied control (117.405-117.475). FSVP (part 1 subpart L) binds the importer — the U.S. owner or consignee at entry (or designated U.S. agent) — for each food imported, requiring a hazard analysis, evaluation/approval of foreign suppliers (reevaluated at least every 3 years), verification activities, corrective actions, importer identification at entry, and records (1.502-1.510). Verification activity menus and the SAHCODHA annual onsite audit default (with written-determination alternative) are parallel (117.410(b)/117.430(b) vs 1.506(d)). Non-duplication: an importer that is a receiving facility complying with Part 117 preventive controls (117.135), 117.136, or a Subpart G supply-chain program for the food is deemed in compliance with FSVP except for 1.509 importer identification (1.502(c)); conversely, a receiving facility that is an importer in compliance with FSVP with documentation of 1.506(e) verification need not conduct Subpart G supplier verification for that raw material (117.405(a)(2)).
